title: Phimosis
intro: Phimosis means the foreskin cannot be pulled back over the tip of the penis. In small boys this is normal and usually resolves by itself as they grow. In older boys and men, a tight foreskin may cause problems and can be treated with creams, stretching or sometimes surgery.

sections.heading: Normal in childhood
paragraphs: At birth, the foreskin is attached to the glans, and it gradually separates over the first years of life. By the age of about three, many boys can retract the foreskin, and the majority can by puberty. Forcing the foreskin back can cause pain, small tears and scarring, which may make the problem worse. Ballooning of the foreskin when urinating can also be normal.

sections.heading: When it is a problem
paragraphs: Concern arises if the foreskin is scarred and white, repeatedly infected, painful when erect, interferes with urination or hygiene, or if the head of the penis is inflamed, a condition called balanitis. In adults, a lack of flexibility can result from infection, skin diseases such as lichen sclerosus or diabetes.

sections.heading: Treatment without surgery
paragraphs: A steroid cream applied to the foreskin for several weeks, together with gentle stretching, often loosens it, both in boys and men. It should be used as advised by the doctor. Good hygiene with warm water and no harsh soaps helps prevent inflammation.

sections.heading: Surgery
paragraphs: If creams do not help or scarring is present, circumcision, removing the foreskin, is the usual operation. Alternatives preserve part of the foreskin by widening it. Circumcision is done under anaesthesia and healing takes a couple of weeks. Risks include bleeding, infection and altered sensation. Parents and patients should discuss the reasons for, and alternatives to, an operation.

sections.heading: Emergency situation
paragraphs: If a retracted foreskin gets stuck behind the head of the penis and cannot be pulled forward, causing swelling and pain, this is called paraphimosis and is an emergency. Seek medical help at once.

examples.title: Reassuring a parent
examples.text: Imagine your three-year-old's foreskin does not retract. You could ask your paediatrician whether this is normal at his age, and agree not to pull on it.

examples.title: Considering treatment
examples.text: Suppose a teenager has pain with a tight foreskin. You might ask about steroid cream and stretching first, and about what an operation would involve if it fails.

questions: Is this phimosis normal for my child's age, or does it need treatment?
How should I use a steroid cream and stretching, and for how long?
